title: Trials, Wisdom, and Doers of the Word
summary: James greets the scattered people of God and tells them to count their trials as joy, because tested faith produces perseverance and maturity. He urges them to ask God for wisdom without doubting, reminds rich and poor of their true standing, and insists that temptation comes from our own desires, while every good gift comes from the unchanging Father. Believers must be quick to listen, slow to anger, and doers of the word, whose religion shows in controlled speech, care for orphans and widows, and a life unstained by the world.
story: James opens the letters that follow Paul's in the New Testament, and it takes us back to the life of the earliest Jewish believers in Jesus. The church had begun in Jerusalem at Pentecost, and persecution scattered many of its members (Acts 8:1; 11:19). James, the brother of Jesus and leader of the Jerusalem church, writes to believers living under pressure, poorer than their neighbors and tempted to let hardship sour their faith or wealth divide their assemblies. This first chapter introduces nearly every subject the letter will develop: trials and endurance, wisdom, the rich and the poor, desire and sin, anger and speech, and above all the demand that hearing God's word must lead to doing it.
historical:
The letter is addressed “To the twelve tribes of the Dispersion.” Israel's twelve tribes had long since been scattered by the Assyrian and Babylonian conquests, and by the first century large Jewish communities lived across the Roman Empire and beyond. Using the tribal name for believers in Jesus says that they are the true continuation of Israel, God's people in exile, whether James means Jewish Christians abroad or the whole church. If James the brother of Jesus wrote the letter, as the church's tradition holds, it comes from Jerusalem before his death around AD 62, possibly as early as the 40s. Those decades brought real hardship to Judea: Acts 11:28-30 records a famine in the reign of the emperor Claudius (AD 41-54) during which the church at Antioch sent relief to believers in Judea, and tensions between wealthy landowners and poor laborers ran high.

The opening greeting uses a single Greek word meaning greetings (chairein), the standard opening of a letter in the Greek world. The same word opens the letter sent from the Jerusalem council in Acts 15:23, after James proposed its decision, a small point that some scholars cite in favor of his authorship.
cultural:
James's pictures come from the life of the eastern Mediterranean. The wave of the sea driven by the wind would be familiar to anyone who lived near the coast or crossed the Sea of Galilee. The scorching heat that withers the flower of the field likely refers to the burning east wind (the sirocco) that blows off the desert and can dry up spring vegetation in a day. Mirrors were made of polished bronze or other metal and gave a dim, imperfect image, but they were enough to show a person a dirty face that needed washing.

The firstfruits of verse 18 were the first portion of the harvest, offered to God at the Feast of Weeks and other occasions as a sign that the whole harvest was his (Leviticus 23:9-21). Calling believers “a kind of firstfruits of His creation” means they are the first sign of God's coming renewal of everything. Orphans and widows were the most exposed people in ancient society, without a man to provide legal protection or income, and the law of Moses and the prophets repeatedly command care for them (Deuteronomy 10:18; 24:17-21; Isaiah 1:17). By naming them, James defines true religion in the prophets' terms.
literary: James links his sayings by repeated words, a technique found in Jewish wisdom writing. The Greek greeting chairein (verse 1) leads to chara, joy (verse 2); lacking nothing (verse 4) leads to if anyone lacks wisdom (verse 5); the one who perseveres under trial (verse 12) leads to the discussion of being tempted, the same word in Greek (verse 13). The chapter moves through several short units: trials and maturity (2-4), prayer for wisdom (5-8), rich and poor (9-11), trial and temptation (12-18), and hearing and doing (19-27). A cluster of vivid similes (the wave, the fading flower, the mirror) makes abstract warnings concrete. The closing verses 26-27 act as a thesis for what follows: controlled speech (chapter 3), care for the needy (chapter 2), and separation from the world's values (chapter 4).

outline.t: Joy in trials that produce perseverance
Asking God for wisdom in faith
The lowly exalted and the rich brought low
Trial, temptation, and the good gifts of the Father
Religion that is pure and undefiled

doctrines.note: James does not call trials pleasant but tells believers to regard them with joy because of what God does through them: “the testing of your faith develops perseverance”, and perseverance leads to maturity. Suffering endured in faith has a purpose and an end, the crown of life.
Wisdom is God's gift, given “generously to all without finding fault” to anyone who asks in faith. For James wisdom is practical, the skill of living rightly before God, especially under pressure.

God is utterly good and unchanging: “the Father of the heavenly lights, with whom there is no change or shifting shadow.” He tempts no one, gives every good gift, and by his own will gives new birth through the word of truth.
Faith that hears but does not act deceives itself. The one who looks into “the perfect law of freedom” and keeps doing it is blessed. This anticipates the argument of chapter 2.

words.note: Peirasmos, which can mean a trial or test from outside and also a temptation to sin from within. James uses it in verses 2 and 12 for trials that test faith, while the related verb in verses 13-14 means being tempted. The shift is deliberate: the same hardship can become an occasion for growth or for sin, depending on how one responds, and God is the source of the growth, never of the sin.

Dipsuchos, double-minded, literally two-souled. This word is not found in any surviving Greek writing before James and may have been coined in Jewish-Christian circles. It describes a person divided in loyalty, who prays to God while hedging bets elsewhere. It returns in 4:8 and names the divided heart that James treats as the root problem of his readers.

Poiētēs, a doer or maker (the source of the English word poet). “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only” is the chapter's central command. The doer of the word is contrasted with the forgetful hearer, echoing Jesus' parable of the two builders (Matthew 7:24-27).

Thrēskeia, religion, the outward practice of worship and piety. James does not dismiss religious practice but says it is worthless if the tongue is unbridled, and that the religion God approves is care for orphans and widows and personal purity.

christ: James names “the Lord Jesus Christ” in his first verse and calls himself Christ's servant, a striking title from a man who, according to the Gospels, did not believe in his brother during his ministry (John 7:5). Much of the chapter echoes Jesus' own teaching. The promise that God gives wisdom to those who ask recalls “ask and it will be given to you” (Matthew 7:7). The call to be mature and complete recalls Jesus' call to be perfect as the Father is perfect (Matthew 5:48). The blessing on the one who perseveres under trial sounds like the Beatitudes, and the warning to hearers who do not act echoes the parable of the wise and foolish builders. The word of truth that gives new birth and is planted in believers is, for the New Testament, the gospel of Christ (compare 1 Peter 1:23-25). James shows Christ as the Lord whose teaching forms the whole life of his people.

hard.q: If God cannot tempt anyone, what about the times Scripture says God tested people, like Abraham?
hard.a: Genesis 22:1 says that God tested Abraham, and the Greek Old Testament uses the same verb James uses here. The difference lies in purpose and source. A test, in the Bible's sense, is God proving and strengthening faith, as a refiner tests metal to show it is genuine. A temptation is an enticement to sin, and James says its source is our own desire: “each one is tempted when by his own evil desires he is lured away and enticed.” God allows and even brings trials, but he never aims at a person's fall, and he never supplies the evil desire that turns a trial into sin. Some readers find this distinction too neat, since the Bible also describes God using even evil for his purposes (Genesis 50:20). The Christian tradition has generally held both truths: God is sovereign over every circumstance, and God is never the author of sin. James's pastoral point is simple: when you are tempted, do not blame God. Look at the desire within and at the good gifts that come from above.

questions: Think of a trial you have faced. What did it produce in you, and what might it have produced if you had faced it differently?
Where are you most tempted to be a hearer of God's word without being a doer?
James defines pure religion in terms of the most vulnerable. Who are the orphans and widows in your community, and what would caring for them look like?
